newsitem.title: MEXICO: Telmex sees flat rate on nat'l long-distance calls.
newsitem.headline: Telmex sees flat rate on nat'l long-distance calls.

text.p: Mexican telephone giant Telmex will charge one uniform rate for national long-distance calls as of next year, when long-distance competition in Mexico begins in earnest, the Mexico City daily Reforma reported Wednesday. In an interview with Carlos Slim Helu, chief of Telmex and the Grupo Carso holding company that controls Telmex, Reforma said the rate would be 2.26 pesos per minute for residential customers.
Certain customers would be eligible for a 12 percent discount, while clients who run up bills of more than 150 pesos per month would be eligible for an additional 20 percent discount, Reforma said.

Telmex, a former state company and long-time monopoly, started facing competition for business clients in August and will begin competing for residential customers with nine new companies as of January 1, 1997.
"We knew we were going to have to compete, and it is not in our interest to wait," Slim told Reforma in explaining the rate cut.
Telmex also will provide discounts of 20 percent to 38 percent for business clients, who if they stay with Telmex can lock themselves in to the lower rates for three years, Reforma said.

One of Telmex's main competitors, Avantel, a joint venture between MCI Communications Corp and Mexican bank Banamex, announced last month that it too will apply flat-rate charges to domestic long-distance calls but also on international calls.
Avantel will charge one and two pesos per minute for nighttime and daytime domestic long-distance calls, respectively, that are made from residential phones.
Daytime calls to the United States will cost five and seven pesos per minute, respectively, from the north and south of Mexico, and 3.5 pesos and five pesos at night.

In the Reforma interview, Slim said Telmex's main competition would come from MCI and AT&T, which is part of the Alestra consortium that includes several other heavyweight foreign and Mexican companies.
Slim hinted that Telmex might seek to compete in the United States.

"The foreign companies have achieved a lot, entering the (Mexican) market freely, and creating a vote so that users can choose between them and us," Slim said. "Now we want to have the same kind of vote there (in the United States)."

Today's Telmex users will be able to choose a primary long-distance carrier for automatic use but also can select any of the companies for a particular phone call by dialing a special access code for each.
